claim: The Drosophila IP3R shares 60% sequence identity with mammalian IP3Rs
source: The Drosophila IP3R shares 60% sequence identity, similar domain organisation, biophysical and functional properties with mammalian IP3Rs (Chakraborty and Hasan, 2012; Srikanth and Hasan, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Chakraborty and Hasan, 2012; Srikanth and Hasan, 2004)

claim: Three conserved basic residues (R272, K531, and Q533) in the Drosophila IP3R ligand binding domain were mutated to Glutamine to generate IP3RDN
source: Three conserved basic residues in the ligand binding domain (R272, K531, and Q533) of the Drosophila IP3R cDNA were mutated to Glutamine (Q) and the resultant mutant cDNA was used to generate GAL4/UAS inducible transgenic strains (UASItprDN) as described in Materials and methods.
evidence: Described in methods section as experimental procedure performed

claim: IP3R levels were significantly enhanced in fly heads with ItprDN compared to genetic controls
source: IP3R levels were significantly enhanced in fly heads with ItprDN as compared to genetic controls and were equivalent to overexpression of a wild-type IP3R transgene (Itpr+; Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B

claim: vGlutVGN6341 marked neurons expressing IP3RDN exhibit reduced and delayed Ca2+ responses to Carbachol stimulation
source: vGlutVGN6341 marked neurons expressing IP3RDN exhibit reduced as well as delayed Ca2+ responses to Carbachol stimulation as compared to controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP6m fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1C

claim: Attenuated Ca2+ responses were observed in mitochondria upon carbachol stimulation in presence of IP3RDN
source: Similar to cytosolic GCaMP, attenuated Ca2+ responses, that took longer to reach peak values, were observed upon carbachol stimulation in presence of IP3RDN (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by mitoGCaMP measurements shown in Figure 1D

claim: Flies with pan-neuronal nsybGAL4-driven expression of ItprDN exhibit significantly reduced flight bouts
source: Flies with pan-neuronal nsybGAL4-driven expression of ItprDN exhibit significantly reduced flight bouts (281.4 ± 38.9 s) as compared to the appropriate genetic controls ItprDN/+ (773.3 ± 30.4 s) and nsyb/+ (670.6 ± 41.3 s) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by flight assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Stronger flight deficits were obtained by expression of ItprDN in Tyrosine Hydroxylase expressing cells
source: Stronger deficits in flight bout durations (185.2 ± 33.7 s) were obtained by expression of ItprDN in Tyrosine Hydroxylase expressing cells, that include a majority of dopaminergic neurons (THGAL4; Friggi-Grelin et al., 2003), as well as in a dopaminergic neuron subset (260 ± 30.5 s) marked by THD'GAL4 (Liu et al., 2012; Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by flight assay data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: Flight deficits were observed upon overexpression of Itpr+ across all neurons
source: Interestingly, flight deficits were also observed upon overexpression of Itpr+ across all neurons (nsyb >Itpr+; 410 ± 31.6 s; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), all TH-expressing cells (TH >Itpr+; 482.2 ± 41.4 s) and a dopaminergic neuron subset, (THD'>Itpr+; 433.5 ± 35.6 s; Figure 2A), although these were milder than with expression of ItprDN.
evidence: Supported by flight assay data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Significantly reduced flight bouts were observed by knockdown of the IP3R with nsybGAL4, THGAL4, and THD'GAL4
source: Significantly reduced flight bouts, comparable to the flight deficits obtained upon expression of ItprDN, were observed by knockdown of the IP3R with nsybGAL4, THGAL4, and THD'GAL4 (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown flight assay data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Pan-neuronal overexpression of the IP3R rescued short flight bouts partially in 10 out of 30 flies tested
source: Pan-neuronal overexpression of the IP3R (nsyb >Itpr+) rescued short flight bouts partially in 10 out of 30 flies tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Complete rescue of short flight was observed in flies rescued by IP3R overexpression in dopaminergic neurons and their TH-D subsets but not the TH-C' subset
source: Interestingly, complete rescue of short flight was observed in flies rescued by IP3R overexpression in dopaminergic neurons and their TH-D subsets but not the TH-C' subset (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: A partial rescue of long flight bouts was observed from dopaminergic neurons and TH-D subsets
source: When tested for longer flight bouts, a partial rescue from dopaminergic neurons and TH-D subsets was observed (304.2 ± 25.1 s; TH >Itpr+) as compared to control flies (747.8 ± 19.4 s; Figure 2C), suggesting that the IP3R regulates flight bout durations from both dopaminergic and certain non-dopaminergic neurons (Agrawal et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2C and inference from comparison

claim: Flight deficits were observed by expression of IP3RDN in PPL1 DANs projecting to the MB lobes α'2α2, α3, γ1peduncle and γ2α′1
source: Amongst the identified splitGAL4 strains, flight deficits were observed by expression of IP3RDN in PPL1 DANs projecting to the MB lobes α'2α2, α3, γ1peduncle and γ2α′1 (MB504BGAL4), but not with PPL1 DANs projecting to the MB lobes α'2α2, α3, and Y1peduncle (MB438BGAL4; Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 3), suggesting PPL1-γ2α′1DANs as the primary focus of IP3R function.
evidence: Supported by splitGAL4 flight assay data shown in Figure 2E and inference from comparison

claim: Expression of ItprDN in PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs resulted in significantly shorter flight bouts
source: Indeed, expression of ItprDN in PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs, marked by MB296BGAL4, resulted in significantly shorter flight bouts, when compared to Itpr+ expression in the same cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by flight assay data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Flight deficits were observed upon expression of IP3RDN during pupal development and not when expressed in adults
source: Flight deficits were observed upon expression of IP3RDN during pupal development and not when expressed in adults. In pupae the deficit was most prominent by expression of the ItprDN during the shorter window of 48–96 hr APF (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by temporal expression experiment data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Flight in itprku mutant animals was rescued to a significant extent by Itpr+ expression from 48 to 96 hr APF but not when expressed before and after
source: Flight in itprku mutant animals was rescued to a significant extent by Itpr+ expression from 48 to 96 hr APF (277 ± 60.3 s) but not when expressed before and after.
evidence: Supported by temporal rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Post-48 hr APF is the time period during which levels of the IP3R are upregulated in the pupal brain
source: Interestingly, post-48 hr APF is also the time period during which levels of the IP3R are upregulated in the pupal brain (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by western blot data from pupal brain lysates shown in Figure 3C

claim: The number of PPL1 DANs was no different between controls and in flies expressing ItprDN
source: The number of PPL1 DANs was no different between controls and in flies expressing ItprDN in either TH-D or MB296B marked neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Projections from MB296B to the γ2α′1 MB lobes appeared unchanged upon expression of ItprDN
source: Moreover, projections from MB296B to the γ2α′1 MB lobes also appeared unchanged upon expression of ItprDN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Adult flight bouts were significantly shorter upon stage specific knock-down (48–96 hr APF) of the mAChR in TH-D' neurons
source: Adult flight bouts were significantly shorter upon stage specific knock-down (48–96 hr APF) of the mAChR in TH-D' neurons with an RNAi under temporal control of the TARGET system (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by temporal RNAi knockdown flight assay data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Knockdown of mAChR in PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs manifested mild flight defects
source: Further knockdown of mAChR in PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs also manifested mild flight defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown flight assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Loss of synaptic vesicle recycling in pupae resulted in significantly shorter flight bout durations
source: Loss of synaptic vesicle recycling in pupae resulted in significantly shorter flight bout durations of 419.9 ± 50.2 s (THD') and 411.5 ± 57 s (MB296B) as compared to controls (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by Shibirets expression flight assay data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: The requirement for synaptic vesicle release was restricted to 48–96 hr APF
source: The requirement for synaptic vesicle release was further restricted to 48–96 hr APF consistent with the requirement of IP3R at the same time interval (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by temporal Shibirets expression data shown in Figure 4A and comparison with Figure 3A,B

claim: Flight bout durations were reduced significantly after acute inactivation (5 min) of synaptic vesicle recycling in PPL1 DANs and the pair of PPL1-γ2α′1 subset DANs in adults
source: Importantly, flight bout durations were reduced significantly after acute inactivation (5 min) of synaptic vesicle recycling in PPL1 DANs (THD') and the pair of PPL1-γ2α′1 subset (MB296B) DANs in adults, supporting a requirement for neurotransmitter release from these neurons during flight (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by acute Shibirets inactivation flight assay data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The food seeking index of hungry flies with IP3RDN was reduced significantly as compared to controls
source: The food seeking index of hungry flies with IP3RDN was reduced significantly as compared to controls (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—source data 2, Figure 4—video 1 and Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: Supported by food-seeking assay data shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: Knockdown of mAChR in either PPL1 (THD') or PPL1-γ2α′1 decreased the ability of starved males to find a yeast drop
source: Knockdown of mAChR in either PPL1 (THD') or PPL1-γ2α′1 decreased the ability of starved males to find a yeast drop (Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data 3), while fed flies were similar to genetic controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Figure 4—source data 6).
evidence: Supported by food-seeking assay data with mAChR knockdown shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: Fluorescence of Syt.eGFP in the MB lobes was no different between control brains and in presence of the IP3RDN
source: Fluorescence of Syt.eGFP in the MB lobes was no different between control brains and in presence of the IP3RDN (Figure 5A), suggesting that synapse numbers were unchanged by expression of IP3RDN.
evidence: Supported by synaptotagmin-GFP fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 5A and inference from comparison

claim: Responding brains decreased from 77% (10/13 brains) in controls to 47% (8/17 brains) upon expression of IP3RDN
source: Responding brains decreased from 77% (10/13 brains) in controls to 47% (8/17 brains) upon expression of IP3RDN.
evidence: Supported by GRABDA fluorescence response data

claim: GRABDA fluorescence arising from dopamine release was significantly muted amongst responders expressing the IP3RDN as compared to responders from control brains
source: Moreover, GRABDA fluorescence arising from dopamine release was significantly muted amongst responders expressing the IP3RDN as compared to responders from control brains (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by GRABDA fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Increase in GRABDA fluorescence at the synaptic terminals in the MB was faster than the carbachol-stimulated change in GCaMP fluorescence measured in the cell body
source: Interestingly, increase in GRABDA fluorescence at the synaptic terminals in the MB was faster (Figure 5C) than the carbachol-stimulated change in GCaMP fluorescence measured in the cell body as measured by time taken to reach the peak response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by comparison of GRABDA and GCaMP fluorescence kinetics shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Neurons expressing IP3RDN and GCaMP did not evince a significant Ca2+ response either during or after red light stimulus from optogenetic stimulation of CsChrimson
source: In neurons expressing IP3RDN and GCaMP optogenetic stimulation of CsChrimsom did not evince a significant Ca2+ response either during or after the red light stimulus, as compared with the control genotype expressing RFP and GCaMP (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic stimulation and GCaMP imaging data shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: There was an instant decline in Arclight fluorescence in control cells, while cells with IP3RDN showed almost no change in fluorescence after KCl-mediated depolarisation
source: There was an instant decline in Arclight fluorescence in control cells, while cells with IP3RDN showed almost no change in fluorescence after KCl-mediated depolarisation (Figure 6C,D, Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by Arclight voltage sensor imaging data shown in Figure 6C,D

claim: Signaling through the IP3R is required for maintaining excitability of central neuromodulatory dopaminergic neurons
source: Taken together, these observations confirm that signaling through the IP3R is also required for maintaining excitability of central neuromodulatory dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic and depolarization experiments showing reduced excitability with IP3RDN

claim: The dominant negative construct (ItprDN) was designed based on previous studies in mammalian IP3Rs
source: The dominant negative construct (ItprDN) was designed based on previous studies in mammalian IP3Rs (Figure 1A; Alzayady et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alzayady et al., 2016

claim: All monomers in the IP3R tetramer need to bind IP3 for channel opening
source: The mammalian dominant negative IP3R1 gene was based on the finding that all monomers in the IP3R tetramer need to bind IP3 for channel opening (Alzayady et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alzayady et al., 2016

claim: Failure of a single IP3R monomer to bind IP3 renders the resultant IP3R tetramer non-functional
source: Failure of a single IP3R monomer to bind IP3 renders the resultant IP3R tetramer non-functional.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from mammalian IP3R studies

claim: Drosophila IP3Rs are tetrameric
source: Drosophila IP3Rs are also tetrameric suggesting that a similar strategy for generating a dominant-negative IP3R could be used for cell-specific studies of neuronal function and behaviour.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Drosophila IP3R structure

claim: Hypomorphic and heteroallelic combinations of Drosophila IP3R mutants exhibit flight deficits ranging from mild to strong
source: Several hypomorphic and heteroallelic combinations of Drosophila IP3R mutants are viable and exhibit flight deficits ranging from mild to strong, the focus of which lies in aminergic neurons (Banerjee et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Banerjee et al., 2004

claim: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in regulation of neurite growth
source: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in multiple cellular processes including regulation of neurite growth (Takei et al., 1998; Xiang et al., 2002), synaptic plasticity (Fujii et al., 2000; Nishiyama et al., 2000) and more recently pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release (Gomez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takei et al., 1998; Xiang et al., 2002

claim: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in synaptic plasticity
source: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in multiple cellular processes including regulation of neurite growth (Takei et al., 1998; Xiang et al., 2002), synaptic plasticity (Fujii et al., 2000; Nishiyama et al., 2000) and more recently pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release (Gomez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fujii et al., 2000; Nishiyama et al., 2000

claim: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release
source: Studies from ex vivo vertebrate neurons have identified a role for the IP3R in multiple cellular processes including regulation of neurite growth (Takei et al., 1998; Xiang et al., 2002), synaptic plasticity (Fujii et al., 2000; Nishiyama et al., 2000) and more recently pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release (Gomez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gomez et al., 2020

claim: Three IP3R isotypes, IP3R1, 2 and 3 are encoded by mammalian genomes
source: Three IP3R isotypes, IP3R1, 2 and 3 are encoded by mammalian genomes (Furuichi, 1994; Taylor et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Furuichi, 1994; Taylor et al., 1999

claim: IP3R1 is the most prevalent isoform in neurons
source: Of these, IP3R1 is the most prevalent isoform in neurons and is relevant in the context of several neurodegenerative disorders (Terry et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Terry et al., 2018

claim: Human mutations in IP3R1 cause Spinocerebellar ataxia 15 (SCA15), SCA29 and Gillespie syndrome
source: Human mutations in IP3R1 cause Spinocerebellar ataxia 15 (SCA15), SCA29 and Gillespie syndrome (Hasan and Sharma, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hasan and Sharma, 2020

claim: Disease causing IP3R1 mutations impact ER-Ca2+ release when tested in mammalian cell lines
source: Disease causing IP3R1 mutations span different domains but several are clustered in the amino terminal IP3 binding region, from where they impact ER-Ca2+ release when tested in mammalian cell lines (Ando et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ando et al., 2018

claim: A common feature of neurological disorders caused by IP3R1 mutations is loss of motor-coordination or ataxia
source: A common feature of these neurological disorders is loss of motor-coordination or ataxia.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about IP3R1-related neurological disorders

claim: Dendritic expression of the IP3R in Purkinje neurons determines Long Term Depression (LTD)
source: Dendritic expression of the IP3R in Purkinje neurons determines Long Term Depression (LTD), a form of post-synaptic plasticity (Miyata et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyata et al., 2000

claim: A recent study in Drosophila identified the IP3R as an essential component of post-synaptic plasticity required for decoding the temporal order of a sensory cue and a reward stimulus in Mushroom Body neurons
source: Interestingly, a recent study in Drosophila also identified the IP3R as an essential component of post-synaptic plasticity, required for decoding the temporal order of a sensory cue and a reward stimulus, in neurons of a higher brain centre, the Mushroom Body (Handler et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Handler et al., 2019

claim: A pre-synaptic role for the IP3R has been demonstrated in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction
source: A pre-synaptic role for the IP3R has been demonstrated in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (Shakiryanova et al., 2011), motor neurons (Klose et al., 2010) and most recently in axonal projections of Purkinje neurons (Gomez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shakiryanova et al., 2011; Klose et al., 2010; Gomez et al., 2020

claim: Knock-down of the IP3R in serotonergic neurons did not give a flight deficit
source: Knock-down of the IP3R in serotonergic neurons, that form another major subset of the tested monoaminergic neurons, did not give a flight deficit (Sadaf et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sadaf et al., 2012

claim: Mild flight deficits were observed upon RNAi mediated knock down of the IP3R in dopaminergic neurons when tethered flight was tested for 30 s
source: Subsequent studies identified mild flight deficits upon RNAi mediated knock down of the IP3R in dopaminergic neurons (DANs) (Pathak et al., 2015) when tethered flight was tested for 30 s.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pathak et al., 2015

claim: Overexpression of a wild-type cDNA construct can partially rescue flight deficits in itpr mutants when expressed in monoaminergic neurons
source: From previous reports, we know that itpr mutants are flightless and their flight deficit can be rescued partially by overexpression of a wild-type cDNA construct (Itpr+; Venkatesh et al., 2001) in monoaminergic neurons (Banerjee et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Venkatesh et al., 2001; Banerjee et al., 2004

claim: In non-excitable cells Ca2+ release through the IP3R regulates growth, secretion, gene expression, and mitochondrial function
source: In non-excitable cells Ca2+ release through the IP3R regulates a range of cellular events including growth, secretion (Inaba et al., 2014), gene expression (Ouyang et al., 2014), and mitochondrial function (Cárdenas et al., 2010; Bartok et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Inaba et al., 2014; Ouyang et al., 2014; Cárdenas et al., 2010; Bartok et al., 2019

claim: Ca2+ released from the IP3R is taken up by mitochondria
source: Ca2+- released from the IP3R is also taken up by mitochondria (Bartok et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bartok et al., 2019

claim: The residual Ca2+ release observed in the cytosol and mitochondria is attributed to the persistence of some IP3R tetramers with all four wild-type subunits
source: We attribute the residual Ca2+ release observed in the cytosol and mitochondria to the persistence of some IP3R tetramers with all four wild-type subunits, encoded by the native itpr gene.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and knowledge of IP3R tetramer assembly

claim: Specification of central dopaminergic neurons is complete in late larval brains
source: It is known that specification of central dopaminergic neurons is complete in late larval brains (Hartenstein et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hartenstein et al., 2017

claim: Neuronal expression of the mAChR during pupal development is required for adult flight
source: From a previous study, it is known that neuronal expression of the mAChR during pupal development is required for adult flight (Agrawal et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Agrawal et al., 2013

claim: Acetylcholine activates the mAChR on PPL1 DANs of late pupae and/or adults to stimulate Ca2+ release through the IP3R
source: Taken together our data support the idea that acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter, activates the mAChR on PPL1 DANs of late pupae and/or adults to stimulate Ca2+ release through the IP3R.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including mAChR knockdown and IP3RDN expression effects

claim: The 48–96 hr time window of pupal development is when adult neural circuits begin to mature with the formation of synapses
source: The 48–96 hr time window of pupal development is when adult neural circuits begin to mature with the formation of synapses, some of which are eliminated whilst others are strengthened (Akin et al., 2019; Consoulas et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Akin et al., 2019; Consoulas et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2016

claim: Synapse strengthening occurs when pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release leads to post-synaptic excitation/inhibition
source: Synapse strengthening occurs when pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release leads to post-synaptic excitation/inhibition (Andreae and Burrone, 2018; Baines, 2003; Baines et al., 2001; Pang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andreae and Burrone, 2018; Baines, 2003; Baines et al., 2001; Pang et al., 2010

claim: IP3-mediated Ca2+ release might modulate synaptic activity and lead to strengthening of synapses between THD' DANs and their post-synaptic partners during pupal development
source: We hypothesized that IP3-mediated Ca2+ release might modulate synaptic activity and hence lead to strengthening of synapses between THD' DANs and their post-synaptic partners during pupal development.
evidence: Hypothesis based on experimental observations and established knowledge

claim: THD' marked dopaminergic neurons require both synaptic vesicle recycling and IP3-mediated Ca2+ release during late pupal development for their adult function
source: These data suggest that THD' marked dopaminergic neurons require both synaptic vesicle recycling and IP3-mediated Ca2+ release during late pupal development for their adult function.
evidence: Inferred from temporal Shibirets and IP3RDN expression experiments

claim: Impaired synaptic vesicle release from adult PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs reduces the ability of starved flies to identify a food source rapidly
source: Impaired synaptic vesicle release from adult PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs, by expression of Shibirets, also reduces the ability of starved flies to identify a food source rapidly (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: Cholinergic stimulation of IP3/Ca2+ in PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs reduces the motivation for longer flight bouts as well as the motivation to search for food
source: Thus cholinergic stimulation of IP3/Ca2+ in PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs reduces the motivation for longer flight bouts as well as the motivation to search for food.
evidence: Inferred from mAChR knockdown effects on both flight and food-seeking behavior

claim: Expression of IP3RDN in MB296B DANs reduced the synaptic release of dopamine at the γ2α′1 lobe
source: Thus, expression of IP3RDN in MB296B DANs reduced the synaptic release of dopamine at the γ2α′1 lobe.
evidence: Inferred from GRABDA fluorescence measurements showing reduced dopamine release

claim: There exist a greater number of mAChRs near the synapse than on the soma of MB296B DANs
source: Perhaps, there exist a greater number of mAChRs near the synapse than on the soma of MB296B DANs.
evidence: Speculated based on faster GRABDA response compared to somatic GCaMP response

claim: mAChRs are present on the processes of Kenyon cells in the mushroom body
source: For example, mAChRs are also present on the processes of Kenyon cells in the mushroom body (Bielopolski et al., 2019; Kondo et al., 2020) and form a tripartite synapse with dendrites from MB output neurons (MB-ONs) and axonal processes of MB296B DANs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bielopolski et al., 2019; Kondo et al., 2020

claim: The neurotransmitter acetylcholine stimulates dopamine release in adult DANs through mAChR-IP3R signaling
source: Although requirement for the IP3R and the mAChR was restricted to 48–96 hr APF, these data suggest that the neurotransmitter acetylcholine stimulates dopamine release in adult DANs through mAChR-IP3R signaling.
evidence: Inferred from GRABDA experiments showing carbachol-stimulated dopamine release

claim: The lack of flight deficits by adult-specific expression of IP3RDN and knockdown of mAChR is probably due to perdurance of the respective proteins from late pupae through to adults
source: The lack of flight deficits by adult-specific expression of IP3RDN (Figure 3A) and knockdown of mAChR (Figure 3D) is probably due to perdurance of the respective proteins from late pupae through to adults.
evidence: Speculated based on temporal expression patterns and protein stability

claim: Reduced strength of MB synapses by pupal expression of IP3RDN and concomitant inhibition of synaptic vesicle release during circuit maturation may contribute to adult flight deficits
source: It remains possible that reduced strength of MB synapses, by pupal expression of IP3RDN and concomitant inhibition of synaptic vesicle release during circuit maturation, also contribute to adult flight deficits.
evidence: Speculated as an alternative or additional mechanism

claim: PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs are likely to receive direct excitatory inputs in addition to neuromodulatory input of acetylcholine
source: In addition to the neuromodulatory input of acetylcholine, the PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs are likely to receive direct excitatory inputs.
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic and depolarization experiments

claim: Some MB296B neurons exhibit high basal activity even in the absence of optogenetic stimulation
source: In agreement with recent findings, some MB296B neurons exhibit high basal activity even in the absence of optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Siju et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to Siju et al., 2020

claim: Neurons with IP3RDN fail to respond to a depolarising stimulus
source: These data suggest that neurons with IP3RDN fail to respond to a depolarising stimulus.
evidence: Inferred from KCl depolarization and optogenetic stimulation experiments

claim: A role for the PPL1 cluster of dopaminergic neurons in modulating flight and longer flight bouts has been reported earlier
source: Although insect flight is an innate behaviour the persistence of flight requires motivation presumably driven by neuromodulatory mechanisms and circuits in the central brain, that need to intersect with hard-wired flight circuits in the ventral ganglion. A role for the PPL1 cluster of dopaminergic neurons in modulating flight and longer flight bouts has been reported earlier (Pathak et al., 2015; Ravi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pathak et al., 2015; Ravi et al., 2018

claim: This is the first report identifying the two PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs as required for maintenance of flight
source: However, amongst the PPL1 cluster this is the first report identifying the two PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs as required for maintenance of flight.
evidence: Claimed as novel finding from this study

claim: The PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs and their downstream Mushroom body output neuron (MBON- γ2α′1) encode the state of hunger
source: The PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs and their downstream Mushroom body output neuron (MBON- γ2α′1) also encode the state of hunger (Tsao et al., 2018), formation and consolidation of appetitive memory (Berry et al., 2018; Felsenberg et al., 2017; Yamazaki et al., 2018), fat storage (Al-Anzi and Zinn, 2018), and sleep (Aso et al., 2014b; Sitaraman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tsao et al., 2018; Berry et al., 2018; Felsenberg et al., 2017; Yamazaki et al., 2018; Al-Anzi and Zinn, 2018; Aso et al., 2014b; Sitaraman et al., 2015

claim: Dopamine release from PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs increased in starved flies
source: These studies identified the importance of modulated dopamine release as a motivational cue wherein dopamine release from PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs increased in starved flies (Tsao et al., 2018) and inhibited the activity of a cholinergic output neuron from the Mushroom Body (MBON- γ2α′1; Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: The MBON- γ2α′1 projects to PAM neurons, the fan shaped body (FSB) and the lateral accessory lobe (LAL)
source: The MBON- γ2α′1 projects to another set of central DANs, the PAM neurons (Felsenberg et al., 2017), identified as flight promoting in a previous study (Manjila et al., 2019), as well as the fan shaped body (FSB) and the lateral accessory lobe (LAL; Scaplen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Felsenberg et al., 2017; Manjila et al., 2019; Scaplen et al., 2020

claim: Continuous sensory inputs are essential for flight and may reach PPL1- γ2α′1/MBON - γ2α′1 synapses through cholinergic Kenyon cells
source: In addition, continuous sensory inputs are essential for flight and these may reach PPL1- γ2α′1/MBON - γ2α′1 synapses through cholinergic Kenyon cells (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017 and inference about circuit connectivity

claim: Carbachol-stimulated Dopamine release at the MB-γ2α′1 lobe may in part be post-synaptic to acetylcholine release from the Kenyon cells
source: In this context, carbachol-stimulated Dopamine release at the MB-γ2α′1 lobe may in part be post-synaptic to acetylcholine release from the Kenyon cells.
evidence: Speculated based on circuit connectivity and experimental observations

claim: LAL neurons signal to descending neurons that presumably connect with the flight circuit in the ventral ganglion
source: Amongst these the LAL neurons signal to descending neurons (Namiki et al., 2018; Namiki and Kanzaki, 2016) that presumably connect with the flight circuit in the ventral ganglion.
evidence: Supported by citations to Namiki et al., 2018; Namiki and Kanzaki, 2016 and inference about circuit connectivity

claim: LAL neurons in locusts exhibit flight correlated activity changes
source: This idea is broadly supported by the observation that LAL neurons in locusts exhibit flight correlated activity changes (Homberg, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Homberg, 1994

claim: The FSB processes visual inputs for flight navigation
source: The FSB processes visual inputs for flight navigation (Weir and Dickinson, 2015) and functions during turning behaviour (Shiozaki et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Weir and Dickinson, 2015; Shiozaki et al., 2020

claim: In cockroaches, activation of the FSB induces turns
source: In cockroaches, activation of the FSB induces turns (Guo and Ritzmann, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo and Ritzmann, 2013

claim: The PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs receive inputs for assessing the internal state through multiple GPCRs including sNPFR, Insulin receptor, AstA receptor and a serotonin receptor 5HT1B
source: The PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs receive inputs for assessing the internal state through multiple GPCRs including certain neuropeptide receptors such as sNPFR, Insulin receptor and AstA receptor and a serotonin receptor 5HT1B (Albin et al., 2015; Hergarden et al., 2012; Root et al., 2011; Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Albin et al., 2015; Hergarden et al., 2012; Root et al., 2011; Tsao et al., 2018

claim: Each of the GPCR signals appear to integrate hunger with food seeking behaviour
source: Each of these signals appear to integrate hunger with food seeking behaviour (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: Modulated activity in the PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs serves as a 'sensor' followed by inhibition of MBON - γ2α′1, that forms an important multisensory 'integrating component' for control of downstream 'effector' circuits
source: We propose that modulated activity in the PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs serves as a 'sensor' followed by inhibition of MBON - γ2α′1, that forms an important multisensory 'integrating component' for control of downstream 'effector' circuits.
evidence: Proposed model based on integration of experimental findings and literature

claim: Appropriate MBON- γ2α′1 outputs are required to maintain long flight bouts, similar to the maintenance of wakefulness and increase in the search for food when hungry
source: Appropriate MBON- γ2α′1 outputs are required to maintain long flight bouts, similar to the maintenance of wakefulness (Aso et al., 2014b; Sitaraman et al., 2015) and increase in the search for food when hungry (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from experimental results and supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014b; Sitaraman et al., 2015; Tsao et al., 2018

claim: Genetic manipulations that target intracellular calcium signaling are known to affect the intrinsic excitability of neurons
source: Genetic manipulations that target intracellular calcium signaling are known to affect the intrinsic excitability of neurons.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claim: Purkinje neurons in mice with cell-specific knockout of the ER-Ca2+ sensor Stim1 exhibit a decreased frequency of firing
source: For example, Purkinje neurons in mice with cell-specific knockout of the ER-Ca2+ sensor Stim1, that functions downstream of mGluR1, exhibit a decreased frequency of firing (Ryu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryu et al., 2017

claim: In Drosophila FMRFa Receptor mediated calcium signaling modulates the excitability of PPL1 dopaminergic neurons through CAMKII
source: In Drosophila FMRFa Receptor mediated calcium signaling modulates the excitability of PPL1 dopaminergic neurons through CAMKII (Ravi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ravi et al., 2018

claim: Reduced excitability of dopaminergic neurons expressing the IP3RDN transgene supports a role for intracellular calcium signals in setting the threshold of membrane excitability in response to neuromodulatory signals
source: Reduced excitability of dopaminergic neurons expressing the IP3RDN transgene (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) further supports a role for intracellular calcium signals in setting the threshold of membrane excitability in response to neuromodulatory signals, such as acetylcholine (this study), the FMRFa neuropeptide (Ravi et al., 2018), and glutamate (Ryu et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and supported by citations

claim: Knock-down of the IP3R in Drosophila larval neurons alters their expression profile and specifically affects the expression of several membrane localised ion-channels
source: In addition to the direct activation of Ca2+-dependant enzymes such as CamKII, previous reports have shown that knock-down of the IP3R in Drosophila larval neurons alters their expression profile and specifically affects the expression of several membrane localised ion-channels (Jayakumar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jayakumar et al., 2018

claim: Reduced translation of proteins due to IP3R knockdown has been demonstrated in peptidergic neurons
source: Reduced translation of proteins due to IP3R knockdown has also been demonstrated in peptidergic neurons (Megha and Hasan, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Megha and Hasan, 2017

claim: Changes in membrane excitability could derive from direct regulation of ion channels by Ca2+ and Ca2+ dependant enzymes as well as an altered density of specific ion channels
source: Changes in membrane excitability could thus derive from direct regulation of ion channels by Ca2+ and Ca2+ dependant enzymes as well as an altered density of specific ion channels.
evidence: Inferred from previous studies and experimental observations

claim: Both direct and indirect effects of ER-Ca2+ on synaptic vesicle release have been observed in vertebrates and Drosophila
source: Both direct and indirect effects of ER-Ca2+ on synaptic vesicle release have been observed in vertebrates (Gomez et al., 2020; Rossi et al., 2008; Sharma and Vijayaraghavan, 2003) and Drosophila (James et al., 2019; Klose et al., 2010; Richhariya et al., 2018; Shakiryanova et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gomez et al., 2020; Rossi et al., 2008; Sharma and Vijayaraghavan, 2003; James et al., 2019; Klose et al., 2010; Richhariya et al., 2018; Shakiryanova et al., 2011

claim: mAChR stimulated ER-Ca2+ signals through the IP3R regulate synaptic release of dopamine from PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs during circuit maturation and during adult flight
source: Because short flight bouts are also observed upon acute inhibition of vesicle recycling in adults our data support a model where mAChR stimulated ER-Ca2+ signals through the IP3R regulate synaptic release of dopamine from PPL1- γ2α′1 DANs during circuit maturation and during adult flight.
evidence: Proposed model based on integration of experimental findings
